This post is one of those few times that I just don’t have the words to describe what I’m trying to say - so I will end with this. I had been a Marine Corps prosecutor for several years before I was selected to deploy to combat with 1/8. I had seen the dark underbelly of the Marine Corps - court-martialing and convicting Marines, ensuring they paid for their crimes. And I saw some of the worst the Marine Corps had. I’ve sent Marines away for literally decades of confinement at Fort Leavenworth for their heinous criminal actions. So, by the time I found out I would be joining an infantry battalion, my soul ached - I had only seen the worst. The sordid. The incomprehensible. The indescribable. The “don’t ever tell these stories in polite company”. My soul literally hurt. Where were the Marines I had read about, heard about and seen captured on video from fights and battles long past in the Corps’ illustrious history? Did those Warriors even exist anymore? Then..... Then I went to war with the finest Warriors of the Marine Corps. I met men like Pj Stevens, Kris Quintana, Joe Watkins, Craig Rizzo, Ben Alicea, Allen Hayden, Anthony Silva, Tom Tribou and the Marine Corps’ best Sergeant Major, Anthony Hope. Facebook won’t let me tag them all, but I counted - and there are about 990 more Warriors of 1/8 I could tag. And my soul was refreshed. These were the men of lore. The men of legend. The men of honor. Courage. Integrity. Strength. Valor. Selflessness. Humility. Men of renown. If you ask them today, not one of them will call themselves a hero. Not one of them will pound their chest. Not one of them will brag about their war exploits that November. So, I will do it for them. Because these I listed represent the Shaun O'Neal, James David Maxey III, Derek Fry, Kelley Starling, Ignacio Rufino and Robby Landers’ of 1/8. Men who daily put their lives on the line. For our Country. For freedom. For Liberty. And for each other. They made the impossible look routine. They made the heroic look ordinary. Men who now quietly go about their lives, loving their families, enjoying their hobbies and life in general, loving their Country and always remembering The Brotherhood. But the men of 1/8 should be recognized and remembered for their heroism, gallantry and fight. I was invited recently to a reunion of some of these Marines who are going to get together out in the woods and rough it for a long weekend. I can’t describe how much I wish I could go and enjoy the company, stories, mead and meat - to be in the presence of those I trusted with my life. Because I was a young Captain back in 2004. When I attached to 1/8, I had only been a Captain for 8 days. I knew very little about the broader Marine Corps and next to nothing about fighting with an infantry battalion in combat. I figured all that out on my own. But I knew - quickly - that I would be fighting with good men. That I was going to battle alongside the (mostly) quiet Warriors of legend. And I departed 1/8 fourteen months later with a full soul and my faith in what it means to be a Marine restored. I finally knew in my heart that all of the myths and stories of battles long ago were accurate. United States Marines are The Few - The Proud. And these young men are the finest Warriors this Nation has ever had. So, this November, I not only remember the 21 Marines of 1/8 who fell, and honor their memory, I recognize the valor and heroism of all of 1/8 who fought. On November 7, 2004, when the Battle of Fallujah struck with the crushing crescendo of the MCLIC that blasted the entry into Fallujah, I know that all of Valhalla silently stood in awe to watch the Warriors of 1/8 in action. And, as each of our Warriors fell in that battle, they were met with resounding cheers by all who had preceded them. They were welcomed into the pantheon of fallen Warriors, to guard the Pearly Gates against any enemy incursion and to forever cheer on those of us not yet with them. Remember the 21. Remember those who stood against the enemy. Remember their valor. Semper Fidelis.
